title: Beijing Ties Rare-Earth Curbs on Japan to 'Remilitarization,' and TSMC Starts Ripping Them Out of Its Fabs
subhead: China's foreign ministry gave its first political justification for squeezing yttrium supplies to Tokyo, while TSMC confirmed it is hunting rare-earth-free motors for its factory tools — the first concrete sign that chipmakers are treating minerals as a supply risk to be engineered out, not managed.

sections.heading: China Gives Its Rare-Earth Curbs on Japan a Political Rationale
sections.body:
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday that export controls on Japan were imposed 'in accordance with laws and regulations' with the aim of preventing Japanese 'remilitarization' and attempts to acquire nuclear weapons, according to Global Times and Anadolu Agency. The statement responded to a Financial Times report that Tokyo has asked Washington and major US companies to press Beijing to ease the restrictions.

The FT reported that Japan could run out of yttrium — used in heat-resistant coatings for jet engines, electronics and semiconductor manufacturing equipment — within months. Beijing cited its standing position that it supports stable global critical-mineral supply chains. According to a 247wallst analysis citing US Geological Survey data, global yttrium oxide mine production in 2025 was roughly 10,000–15,000 tonnes, overwhelmingly from China, and the US has no fully commercial plant to separate or refine it. US yttrium oxide imports fell to zero in May and June 2026, with Reuters reporting 29 tonnes approved for July.

Tokyo has so far described a shortage and made a request; no US commitment, deal or timeline has been announced.
sections.whyItMatters: Turning a licensing dispute into a security argument about Japan's rearmament gives Beijing a justification it can repeat elsewhere. It also signals the curbs are political rather than technical, which makes them harder for importers to plan around.

sections.heading: TSMC Asks Suppliers for Motors Without Rare-Earth Magnets
sections.body:
TSMC is exploring alternatives to rare-earth components in its factory equipment — specifically, motors that do not require rare-earth magnets in its automated fabs — according to Reuters (via Taiwan News), citing three people familiar with the matter. The company has asked suppliers whether such motors can be built for its production lines.

The target is not just the chips themselves but the machinery that moves wafers: rare-earth permanent magnets sit inside the drive systems and robotics of a modern fab. A leading-edge plant runs thousands of these units, and each is a maintenance item subject to import licensing.

The sourcing problem is a long one — automotive motor designs have been shifting away from rare-earth magnets for years, but fab-grade precision and reliability requirements are stricter, and replacing installed equipment is a multi-year capital program.
sections.whyItMatters: Most mineral-supply coverage focuses on magnets for cars and defence. TSMC looking at its own motors shows the exposure reaches into the tooling of the most advanced fabs — and that at least one major chipmaker has started treating mineral risk as an engineering problem rather than a diplomatic one.

sections.heading: OpenAI Goes Quiet on China Chip Limits Ahead of the Lame-Duck Fight
sections.body:
OpenAI has stopped advocating for strict US limits on advanced chip sales to China, according to Politico, as relayed by The Next Web (which notes it has not independently verified the reporting). Capitol Hill aides and lobbyists told Politico the company's position has become 'a bit more fuzzy'; one aide said 'silence is doing Nvidia's work for it.'

The timing matters. China hawks in Congress want to attach new chip restrictions to the annual defence spending bill and plan to push in the lame-duck session after the midterms — and had counted OpenAI as a prominent industry ally. Anthropic has moved the other way, backing several chip bills and leaving a major tech trade group in September over its push to soften them.

The ties are financial as much as political: Nvidia finalised a $30bn equity investment in OpenAI in February, and under an August deal agreed to be sole chip supplier at an Ohio data centre OpenAI will lease, guaranteeing up to $105bn for its first phase.
sections.whyItMatters: The lobby lineup on export controls is consolidating around the president's position. That removes one of the few AI-lab voices arguing for tighter curbs just as Congress tries to legislate them.

sections.heading: Micron's Taoyuan Workers Stage Taiwan's First Chip-Industry Strike
sections.body:
A Micron Technology labour union staged Taiwan's first-ever strike in the semiconductor industry on Thursday, Nikkei Asia reported, in a dispute over bonuses and profit-sharing that workers say have not reflected record AI-driven memory profits. The Taoyuan union had voted 99% to authorise action and announced a one-day strike on October 22, per Reuters.

Taoyuan is Micron's largest manufacturing hub. The union rejected a pay offer as talks continue, according to ad-hoc-news reporting on the company's position.
sections.whyItMatters: Memory is the tightest link in the AI supply chain right now, and Taiwan has long been treated as a labour-cost and labour-peace assumption in chips. A first strike sets a precedent for how the AI windfall gets divided inside the industry's most critical production base.

sections.heading: Alibaba Adds Cloud Regions in Turkey, Finland and the Netherlands
sections.body:
Alibaba Cloud said at its Apsara conference in Hangzhou that it will open its first cloud regions in Turkey, Finland and the Netherlands within 12 months, and expand existing footprints in Malaysia, Germany, the UAE, France and Hong Kong. The buildout sits inside Alibaba Group's roughly $53bn (380bn yuan), three-year AI and cloud infrastructure plan and a target of 20 GW of global capacity by 2032, per Bloomberg, MarketScreener and eWeek.

For context on how crowded that European space is becoming: Google committed at least €13bn ($15.1bn) to AI infrastructure in Finland through 2028 — its largest single European investment — alongside a 22-year power purchase agreement with Fortum, CNBC reported in September.
sections.whyItMatters: Chinese cloud capacity is landing in European jurisdictions at the same time Brussels is tightening rules on high-risk suppliers and building sovereign compute. Data-residency rules will decide whether these regions are usable by European public-sector clients.

sections.heading: EU Telecom Operators Put a €40bn Price Tag on the Huawei Phase-Out
sections.body:
Seventeen European telecom executives — including the CEOs of Orange, Deutsche Telekom and Telefónica — signed an open letter through the Connect Europe lobby warning that a blanket ban on certain non-EU suppliers would impose 'up to €40 billion ($46bn) in replacement costs,' according to AFP via the Economic Times. The letter argues the Cybersecurity Act 'risks draining the sector of the very capital needed for fibre, 5G and 6G.'

The measure sits in the Digital Networks Act, which does not name Chinese vendors but would give operators three years to remove designated 'high-risk' suppliers once identified. It is in negotiation between the European Parliament and the 27 member states.
sections.whyItMatters: The cost estimate is four times the Commission's own figure, per Politico's earlier reporting on industry estimates. That number is now the central argument in the legislative fight — and it will be used to stretch transition periods rather than kill the ban.

sections.heading: Space: Nvidia and SpaceX Line Up Orbital Compute, Amazon Nears Service
sections.body:
SpaceX is targeting Q4 2027 to launch a space-optimised version of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 system — roughly a year earlier than the timeline in its May prospectus, which said orbital data centre satellites could begin deploying 'as early as 2028,' per IBTimes citing Moneywise and Musk's own posts. Nvidia has separately launched a Space-1 Vera Rubin module for orbital data centres, claiming up to 25x the AI compute of an H100 for space-based inference, with Aetherflux, Axiom Space, Kepler, Planet Labs, Sophia Space and Starcloud as users.

SpaceX has said its planned AI satellites could draw about 250 kilowatts at peak and has asked the FCC for authorisation tied to a constellation that could eventually reach as many as one million satellites.

Separately, Amazon has produced its 1,000th Leo satellite at its Kirkland factory and says service launch is weeks away, with completed satellites shipping to Florida every two to three days and hundreds staged at Kennedy Space Center awaiting rockets, per Ars Technica and 425 Business.
sections.whyItMatters: Orbital compute is moving from concept to launch manifest, and the early schedule slip toward 2027 is the first hard date attached to it. Meanwhile Amazon's bottleneck is now launch capacity, not manufacturing — the constraint has flipped.

bottomLine: China's rare-earth squeeze on Japan acquired an explicit political rationale this week, and TSMC responded by asking suppliers for fab motors that need no rare-earth magnets — the first real sign that chipmakers are designing the vulnerability out rather than negotiating around it. On the same days: OpenAI quietly dropped its push for China chip limits ahead of the lame-duck NDAA fight, Taiwan's chip industry saw its first strike at Micron's Taoyuan hub, Alibaba planted cloud regions in Turkey, Finland and the Netherlands, and European telcos put a €40bn price tag on removing Huawei. The common thread is that everyone is now pricing the cost of decoupling — and finding it higher than the political statements suggest.
sources: Global Times, Anadolu Agency, Financial Times, 247wallst, Reuters, Taiwan News, Politico, The Next Web, Nikkei Asia, ad-hoc-news, Bloomberg, MarketScreener, eWeek, CNBC, AFP via Economic Times, IBTimes, Nvidia Newsroom, Ars Technica, 425 Business
